corrections.source_says: Set n_analyzed to null. The manuscript reports 285 participants in the overall experiment, not a distinct analyzed-person count for the Day 2 randomized comparisons or their adjusted regressions. It reports 549 stories, comprising 278 on Day 1 and 271 on Day 2, and says all submitted stories were analyzed. Table 1 separately reports 280 observations for the initial-survey covariates used in the adjusted models. Neither Table S4 nor Table S7 supplies its analyzed-person N. Retain 285 as the reported overall cohort in the descriptive text and retain the day-specific story counts as outputs; do not substitute 271 people solely from the story count. The existing prose caveat is appropriate, but the numeric n_analyzed field still overstates what is reported.
corrections.quote: The experiment involved 285 participants over two days.
corrections.locator: PDF p. 21 (SI p. 5), A.2 Data and Variables, opening paragraph; PDF p. 18 (SI p. 2), A.1, inclusion of all submitted stories; PDF p. 11, Table 1; PDF pp. 48 and 51 (SI pp. 32 and 35), Tables S4 and S7.

confirmed: The main study is a field_rct: students in an elective course on emerging technologies were individually randomly assigned to Human Confirmation, Human Creativity, or Copilot for AI-assisted story writing. The explicit random-assignment statement and Figure S1 establish a randomized comparison of generative-AI configurations, supporting referral to the two-screener pipeline and context_class = none (PDF p. 4, Experimental Design; PDF p. 18, SI A.1; PDF p. 20, Figure S1).

The common no-AI writing task occurred on Day 1 and AI-assisted writing on Day 2. That before/after ordering was fixed; it was not a randomized no-AI control comparison. Human Creativity reserved ideation and outlining for people, Human Confirmation delegated all writing stages to AI, and Copilot allowed collaboration throughout (PDF p. 4; PDF pp. 18-20, SI A.1 and Figure S1).

The reported overall cohort is 285 students. The 549 total stories, including 278 on Day 1 and 271 on Day 2, are outputs; the 2,196 evaluation scores are ratings, not additional participants. Separate numbers at random assignment and per-arm analyzed-person counts are not reported, so the existing null values for those fields are appropriate (PDF pp. 4 and 11, Table 1; PDF pp. 18 and 21, SI A.1-A.2).

Creativity-related outcomes were scored on the produced stories: blinded fellow participants and research assistants evaluated overall quality, originality, interestingness, writing quality, and coherence on a 1-7 scale, with two internal and two external evaluations per story. Computed similarity compared stories across writers (PDF p. 4; PDF p. 19, SI A.1; PDF p. 41, SI B.4; PDF p. 16, Figure 4 caption).

S1-O1 reported statistics are correct: the adjusted Day 2 Human Creativity coefficient relative to Human Confirmation is 0.3376, SE 0.106, with *** denoting p < 0.01. This is a raw overall-quality rating coefficient, not a standardized effect; controls are DAT, writing experience, writing ability, and English proficiency, and the analysis is at the evaluation level (PDF p. 51, Table S7; PDF p. 21, SI A.2.2).

S1-O2 reported statistics are correct: Table S4 gives 0.3031, SE 0.112, *** p < 0.01 for interestingness in its T1 versus T2 row. The note defines the coefficient as the latter group minus the former, so this is Human Creativity minus Human Confirmation, adjusted for the stated individual characteristics at the evaluation level (PDF p. 48, Table S4; PDF p. 22, SI A.2.2).

S1-O3 reported means and intervals are correct: Human Creativity mean = 0.710, 95% CI = [0.700, 0.720]; Human Confirmation mean = 0.779, 95% CI = [0.767, 0.790]. The text calls the differences statistically significant but does not give an exact p value for this pair (PDF p. 7, Content Diversity; PDF p. 15, Figure 4C).

The semantic-similarity measure is cosine similarity between each story embedding and the average embedding of the other stories in its group, using text-embedding-3-large. Its unit is the story/output, and lower similarity represents greater between-writer diversity; the form does not calculate a standardized effect or reverse any printed number (PDF p. 16, Figure 4C caption).

The one_line_finding matches the source: the main text prints Human Creativity versus Human Confirmation quality difference = 0.34, P < 0.01, and the semantic-similarity means are 0.710 versus 0.779 (PDF p. 5, Writing Quality; PDF p. 7, Content Diversity).

The intervention used ChatGPT 3.5 for new 1,000-word stories. The form correctly preserves the source inconsistency between 105-minute writing sessions in the main text and Figure S1 and 75-minute tasks in SI A.1 (PDF p. 4; PDF pp. 18-20, SI A.1 and Figure S1).

The source description is accurate: the local PDF has 57 pages, begins Main Manuscript for, names Kartik Hosanagar and Daehwan Ahn, and contains Supporting Information on PDF pp. 17-57, separately numbered 1-41. No manuscript date or version number is stated in the document; the SI cover lists the MDAR checklist separately, and that checklist is not included (PDF pp. 1, 17 and 57; complete local document).

This is an experimental report, not a synthesis, so synthesis counts and pooled estimates are inapplicable (PDF p. 4, Experimental Design). The original short-form brief explicitly permits up to three main outcomes and defaults in other fields, so the omitted outcome entries and empty extraction fields are not corrections (codex-jobs/lscreen-c793/brief.md, SHORT version instructions).
summary: The paper contains a randomized classroom study of three ChatGPT collaboration designs and should proceed to the two-screener pipeline. The reported effects and source description are accurate, but 285 is the overall participant count rather than a confirmed analyzed sample size.
